name: Currency Hedging
title: Currency Hedging
answer: Currency hedging is the practice of using financial contracts to reduce the effect of exchange rate moves on a company's cash flows, earnings, or balance sheet. In treasury and liquidity work, it covers forecasted transactions, firm commitments, intercompany loans, and foreign currency balances. The scope includes deciding which exposures to hedge, how much to hedge, and over what horizon, often guided by a written policy. It also includes the accounting treatment, because hedge accounting can change when gains and losses appear in the financial statements.

sections.body: Currency hedging is the practice of using financial contracts to reduce the effect of exchange rate moves on a company's cash flows, earnings, or balance sheet. In treasury and liquidity work, it covers forecasted transactions, firm commitments, intercompany loans, and foreign currency balances. The scope includes deciding which exposures to hedge, how much to hedge, and over what horizon, often guided by a written policy. It also includes the accounting treatment, because hedge accounting can change when gains and losses appear in the financial statements.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on treasury management systems, ERP modules, and spreadsheets that hold exposure data, trade details, and valuation inputs. Market data feeds provide spot rates, forward points, and volatility surfaces, while confirmation and settlement systems connect to banks and trading venues. Many teams also use data warehouses or cloud platforms to combine ledger balances, forecast data, and risk positions. AI tools may sit alongside these systems for anomaly detection, cash flow forecasting, or natural language queries over policy documents.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with identifying and measuring exposures from accounting and forecast data, then mapping them to hedgeable risk. Teams apply hedge ratios and tenor rules from policy, execute forwards, options, or swaps, and record the trades in the treasury system. They test effectiveness, measure ineffectiveness, and prepare journal entries and disclosures for hedge accounting. AI can assist by classifying transactions, predicting exposures, flagging outliers, and drafting documentation, but a human still reviews and approves each hedge.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers policy limits, segregation of duties, counterparty credit risk, and audit trails for every trade and valuation. The site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages, and currency hedging policy often sits within that broader body of compliance work. Teams must document hedge relationships, retain evidence of effectiveness testing, and follow accounting standards such as IFRS 9 or ASC 815 where applicable. Risk committees and internal audit review the program, and any AI used in the process needs explainability, data lineage, and controls.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more automated exposure capture, real-time valuation, and continuous hedge accounting rather than month-end batch runs. AI is likely to improve forecasting of cash flows and currency pairs, and to help teams simulate policy changes against historical and scenario data. At the same time, regulators and auditors are paying closer attention to model risk and to how AI-derived inputs affect financial reporting. The practical result is a hedging process that is faster and more data-driven, but still bounded by policy, accounting rules, and human accountability.
